newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia Socialists still weighing reform benefits.
newsitem.headline: Serbia Socialists still weighing reform benefits.

text.p: Serbia looks set to adopt a privatisation law in June but the ruling Socialist Party (SPS) has still to make clear its views on the sell-offs which may not take place until after elections this year.
"The privatisation ministry agreed not to insist on making the process compulsory and on its immediate implementation," a government source, who asked not to be named, said on Tuesday.
Analysts said a key political decision to reform the country's moribund economy was still lacking and waiting for the SPS to give its final say.

"It is obvious that a political decision (to privatise) has not been made yet. There is still some wandering around. They are still weighing ifs and buts," vice-president of the private Braca Karic University Nebojsa Savic told Reuters.

"For a moment, it seemed the political will was there, but it's obvious that things won't go so smoothly and that the Socialists are still calculating whether privatisation would serve their aims," he added.

Sources close to SPS said there was a deep political disagreement between two factions of the party on whether privatisation could help it score another election victory. Presidential and republican parliament elections are due to take place by the end of this year.
Socialist hard-liners claimed that privatisation would inevitably ruin the party's chances of winning the polls.
"That interpretation is exactly what delayed adoption of the law. And nobody knows whether they will allow or completely stop any further talks on privatisation," an economist said.
Economists cautioned any further delay in privatisation would mean that 1997 is definitely not going to be the year of reforms as promised by Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
Economists said the privatisation law offered by the ministry was better than no law at all.

"Any shortcomings of the proposed document can be improved in practice. But only this law can help the country catch up with other transition economies. Each month lost brings more and more damages to the economy," Savic said.

While waiting on the Socialist Party's Economic Council to give the law a "green light" the expert team was busy preparing a new version which would definitely exclude insurance companies and banks from privatisation and decrease proposed discounts.
Experts have not yet found a satisfactory solution to the problem of frozen hard currency savings.

"Frozen savings will be treated as means of payment but we cannot say in which part of the process exactly. There is also an agreement to use some privatisation receipts to repay the savings," Miroljub Hadzic, deputy privatisation minister, said.
The expected adoption of the privatisation law will not be accompanied by a list of 30-50 strategic companies which are to be transformed and privatised by a special state programme.
"The time between adoption and implementation of the law will be used to draw the list of those companies," a government source said.

Meanwhile, the government was said to be finalising the sale of its only profit-making telecommunications company to raise funds needed for a more regular financing of pensions and wages in months ahead of elections expected by the end of 1997.

The deal is said to be stuck over the mobile telephony part, in which Serbia has only one operator, the joint venture between the state's PTT Srbije and the private Braca Karic company, in which BK controls a 51 percent stake. --Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
